newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa to keep helping new Congo - Mbeki.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa to keep helping new Congo - Mbeki.

text.p: South Africa will continue to help Laurent Kabila's Kinshasa government to overcome the legacies, including total bankruptcy, of Mobutu Sese Seko's 32 years in power, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said on Wednesday.
Mbeki told parliament in Cape Town that South Africa had tried through seven months of mediation to prevent a bloody transition in the former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
A key part of the initiative had been to unite outside governments behind a single strategy for peace and democracy as Kabila's forces marched across the country.

"The mediation process is over, but it is clear that there is a continuing hope that South Africa will contribute to, at least, giving advice as to what might be done to secure the future of this country," he said.
Mbeki said the country's new leader, Laurent Kabila, had told him on Sunday he would inherit a plundered treasury.

"The outgoing prime minister who fled to the (neighbouring) Republic of the Congo, informed Kabila that in fact the state coffers were entirely empty and that the prime minister before him, Kengo wa Dondo, actually took what remained in those state coffers with him," he said.

Mbeki, who played a key role in President Nelson Mandela's attempt to ensure a peaceful transition, said Kabila would submit a detailed request for help after he has named his transitional government.

"There needs to be a broad-based transitional authority, as inclusive as possible of the various political forces in the country, so that you don't have a situation in which the alliance would itself be the sole party in the process of governing Zaire in the transitional period," he said.

Mbeki said Kabila would within a few days announce a transitional authority, measures to ensure free political activity for all parties and dates for the convening of a constitutional assembly to adopt an interim constitution.
Mbeki said Kabila would announce a timetable for elections soon, but he warned that organising them would take longer than some had expected.

He said a European Union team had explored the possibilities for an early election in Zaire last year and had reported problems caused by infrastructure, roads, administration and the unresolved of issue of the nationality of some residents.
"The organisation of those elections is clearly going to be a very difficult matter," he said.
